Pyotr Stolypin: Prime Minister of the Russian Empire from 1906 to 1911. Born in Dresden, in the Kingdom of Saxony, to a prominent Russian aristocratic family, Stolypin became involved in government from his early 20s.
This Oglala Lakota leader won the war that bears his name, making the Lakota the only nation to defeat the U.S. on American soil — who was he?
Red Cloud: Leader of the Oglala Lakota (1822–1909)
Elected in January 2022 after the sudden death of her predecessor, this Maltese politician became the youngest-ever, and first Maltese, president of a major European institution — who is she?
Roberta Metsola: President of the European Parliament since 2022.

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?

Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago. The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was the murder of seven members and associates of Chicago's North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929.

Beginning in August 1998, this conflict drew in nine African nations and roughly 25 armed groups after a Central African president turned against his former Rwandan and Ugandan allies — which conflict?
Second Congo War: 1998–2003 war in central Africa.
A viral video of him scolding sleeping city council members made this Japanese mayor an internet sensation before he placed second in the 2024 Tokyo governor's race — who is he?
Shinji Ishimaru: Japanese politician. Ishimaru ran in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election as an independent, but ultimately lost to incumbent Yuriko Koike.
Known as Madame Chiang, the youngest of a trio of politically influential sisters, she married a Nationalist Chinese leader and shaped his government's foreign relations — who is she?
Soong Mei-ling: Wife of Chiang Kai-shek (1898–2003)
Around 986 he revolted against his father Harald Bluetooth to seize Denmark's throne, and in December 1013 briefly became King of England too — which Viking ruler was it?
Swein Forkbeard: King of Denmark and England (died 1014)
Often appearing as a crow and said to wash the bloodstained clothes of those fated to die in battle, which Irish goddess of war and fate is known as the 'phantom queen'?
The Morrígan: Figure from Irish mythology.
The only person to lead Labour to three consecutive general election victories, this MP for Sedgefield served as UK prime minister from 1997 to 2007 — who is he?
Tony Blair: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1997 to 2007.
The son of Ivan III and Sophia Paleologue, this Grand Prince of Moscow annexed Pskov and Ryazan and captured Smolensk from Lithuania during his reign from 1505 to 1533 — who was he?
Vasili III of Russia: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1505 to 1533.
This German industrialist who organized the WWI war economy became foreign minister and negotiated the 1922 Treaty of Rapallo, only to be assassinated months later — who was he?
Walther Rathenau: German businessman and politician (1867–1922)
Starting in his father's grocery business, this English industrialist built an empire on Sunlight Soap and brands like Lux and Lifebuoy through the firm he founded with his brother — who was he?
William Lever, 1st Viscount Leverhulme: English industrialist, philanthropist and politician (1851–1925)

Sparked by rising fuel prices and an online petition with nearly a million signatures, these weekly French demonstrations began in November 2018, their protesters named for the high-visibility garment they wore. What movement was it?
Yellow vests protests: 2018 social movement started in France.

A civil engineer who once ran state transport and construction firms, this member of Macron's Renaissance party became only the second woman to be France's Prime Minister — and the first in 30 years. Who is she?
Élisabeth Borne: Prime Minister of France from 2022 to 2024.
Who among these was born first?
Georges Dumézil (born 1898) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these came out first?
TeX (published 1978) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Vikram Sarabhai is a physicist. Often regarded as the "Father of Indian space program", Sarabhai was honored with Padma Bhushan in 1966 and the Padma Vibhushan (posthumously) in 1972.
Who among these is a chemist?
Glenn T. Seaborg is a chemist. Throughout his career, Seaborg worked for arms control.
What is the atomic number of Beryllium?
Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
In what year was Henk Rogers born?
Henk Rogers is a Dutch-born American video game designer and entrepreneur.
In what year was Ptolemy born?
Ptolemy: The first was his astronomical treatise now known as the Almagest, originally entitled Mathēmatikḗ Syntaxis (Μαθηματικὴ Σύνταξις, 'Mathematical Treatise').
In what year was Michael Burry born?
Michael Burry: Michael James Burry (born June 19, 1971) is an American investor, hedge fund manager, and licensed physician.
In what year did Frank Oppenheimer die?
Frank Oppenheimer: The younger brother of renowned physicist J.
In what year did Hippocrates die?
Hippocrates is also widely recognized for his contributions to medical ethics, being credited with the Hippocratic Oath that remains in use today.
In what year was Oganesson discovered?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
In what year was Arsenic discovered?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
Indometacin: Pfizer. It works by inhibiting the production of prostaglandins, endogenous signaling molecules known to cause these symptoms.
In which country is Blood orange?
Blood orange: Italy. The blood orange is a variety of orange with crimson, near blood-colored flesh.
Who is credited with discovering Iodine?
Iodine: Bernard Courtois. Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
Who is credited with discovering Mendelevium?
Mendelevium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
Who is credited with discovering Magnesium?
Magnesium: Joseph Black. Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
This long-term skin condition occurs when dead skin cells and oil clog hair follicles, producing blackheads, whiteheads, and pimples mainly on the face, chest, and back — what is it?
Acne is a long-term skin condition that occurs when dead skin cells and sebum clog hair follicles.
This Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on welfare economics and has also studied the causes of famines — who is he?
Amartya Sen (born 3 November 1933) is an Indian economist and philosopher.
The largest genus in the arum family with roughly 1,000 species, this flowering plant group is native to the Americas, ranging from northern Mexico down to northern Argentina — which genus?
Anthurium (Schott, 1829) is a genus of about 1,000 species of flowering plants, the largest genus of the arum family, Araceae.

It's one of the oldest natural sciences, recruiting math, physics, and chemistry to explain everything that originates beyond Earth's atmosphere — from comets and quasars to the cosmic microwave background. What field is it?
Astronomy is a natural science that studies celestial objects and the phenomena that occur in the cosmos.

This fluid-dynamics rule holds that a fluid's pressure drops as its speed increases; the Swiss physicist credited with it published the idea in 1738, though Leonhard Euler derived the actual equation — what's it called?
Bernoulli's principle is a key concept in fluid dynamics that relates pressure, speed and height.
Caused by a toxin that thrives in low-oxygen conditions — the same one sold cosmetically as 'botox' — this rare illness brings blurred vision and creeping paralysis but rarely a fever. What is it?
Botulism is a rare and potentially fatal illness caused by botulinum toxin (commonly referred to as botox), which is produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum.

The largest land bird in North America went fully extinct in the wild in 1987 when every survivor was captured for breeding — which critically endangered vulture has since returned to the Grand Canyon and beyond?
California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) is a New World vulture and the largest North American land bird.
This worldwide family of over 5,000 fly species — found everywhere except the Antarctic and Arctic — includes the biting midges also known as sand flies — what is it called?
Ceratopogonidae is a family of flies colloquially known as no-see-ums, sand flies, or biting midges, generally 1-3 millimetres (116-18 in) in length.
An American naturalist who surveyed wildlife in Labrador, he turned what he learned there into quick-freezing methods that launched the modern frozen-food industry. Who was he?
Clarence Birdseye (December 9, 1886 - October 7, 1956) was an American inventor, entrepreneur, and naturalist, who is widely considered the founder of the modern frozen food industry.
Thanks to variations in the OR6A2 gene, some people taste this Mediterranean herb as fresh and citrusy while others swear it tastes like soap — its leaves are called cilantro in the US. What is it?
Coriander is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.

This American nuclear physicist worked on the Manhattan Project and later led the Federation of American Scientists, best remembered for his 1959 testimony that helped sink a controversial cabinet nomination — who is he?
David L. Hill (November 11, 1919 - December 14, 2008) was an American nuclear physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project during World War II and was head of the Federation of American Scientists.
This waterfowl belongs to the same family as swans and geese, but is generally smaller and shorter-necked — and despite the shared family, swans and geese don't count as one. What is it?
Duck is the common name for numerous species of waterfowl in the family Anatidae.
This Italian-American physicist won the 1938 Nobel Prize, built the world's first artificial nuclear reactor (Chicago Pile-1), and is called the "architect of the nuclear age" — who was he?

Enrico Fermi (29 September 1901 - 28 November 1954) was an Italian-American physicist, renowned for being the creator of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, the Chicago Pile-1, and a member of the Manhattan Project.
Immature at birth but developed by puberty, this network of organs includes the vagina, uterus, and fallopian tubes, protected by a fold called the labia majora — what's it called?
Female reproductive system is made up of the internal and external sex organs that function in the reproduction of new offspring.

A French economist who gave lectures up and down the country and helped found the Inter-Parliamentary Union, he shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 for his work in Europe's peace movement — who was he?
Frédéric Passy (20 May 1822 - 12 June 1912) was a French economist and pacifist who was a founding member of several peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
Caused in over 90% of cases by iodine deficiency, this visible swelling in the neck comes from an enlarged thyroid gland — name the condition?
Goitre (British English, spelled goiter in American English) is a swelling in the neck resulting from an enlarged thyroid gland.

A spiny mammal with 17 species across five genera in Europe, Asia, and Africa, this creature shares distant ancestry with shrews. There are no native populations in Australia or the Americas, though one extinct genus once roamed North America—what is it?
Hedgehog is a spiny mammal of the subfamily Erinaceinae, in the eulipotyphlan family Erinaceidae.
A colourless, ammonia-scented liquid with formula N2H4, this hazardous compound foams polymers, inflates airbags, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula N2H4.
Lasting anywhere from a few days to over a month, this disorder makes it hard to fall or stay asleep, leaving daytime drowsiness, irritability and trouble focusing in its wake — what is it?
Insomnia is a sleep disorder causing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep for as long as desired.
This American physicist revived general relativity in postwar America and had a knack for naming things — coining "quantum foam," "wormhole," and the term "black hole" itself. Who is he?
John Archibald Wheeler (July 9, 1911 - April 13, 2008) was an American theoretical physicist.

Normally part of the healthy flora in the mouth, skin, and gut, this rod-shaped bacterium can turn destructive if aspirated into the lungs, producing a telltale bloody, brick-colored jelly-like sputum — what's the organism?
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
Viruses muddy its definition, and it might exist beyond Earth in unfamiliar forms — but on this planet it fills air, water and soil, even harsh niches of extremophiles. What is it?
Life is the capacity, in matter, for processes such as cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, cell growth, adaptation, response to stimuli, and reproduction.
This alpha-amino acid, a building block for many proteins, carries a side chain that stays partially charged at the body's normal pH, classifying it among the basic amino acids — what is it?
Lysine (symbol Lys or K) is an -amino acid that is a precursor to many proteins.
A German historian, jurist, and political economist born in 1864, he is counted among the central founders of sociology and still shapes social theory today — who was he?

Max Weber (21 April 1864 - 14 June 1920) was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist who was one of the central figures in the development of sociology and the social sciences more generally.
Widowed in 2021, this Israeli-American billionaire physician publishes Israel Hayom and has been among the most prominent financial supporters of a US president since 2016 — who is she?
Miriam Adelson (ne Farbstein; born October 10, 1945) is an Israeli-American physician, businesswoman, philanthropist, and conservative political donor.
This protective plate at fingertips and toe-tips is found in nearly every primate except marmosets, and is made of the same tough protein found in claws, hooves, and horns — what is it?

Nail (anatomy) is a protective plate characteristically found at the tip of the digits (fingers and toes) of almost all primates (except for marmosets), corresponding to the claws in other tetrapod animals.
Built from nucleotide units of a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base, these biomolecules come in two main classes distinguished by whether their sugar is ribose or deoxyribose — what are they?
Nucleic acid are large biomolecules that are crucial in all cells and viruses.
Belonging to the pea family and native to Mesoamerica, this vine produces blue or white flowers and an edible tuberous root known in Spanish as jícama — which species?
Pachyrhizus erosus (from Nahuatl languages: xicamatl) or Mexican turnip, is a native Mesoamerican vine, although the name jicama most commonly refers to the plant's edible tuberous root.

Nicknamed with the backronym 'Practical Extraction and Reporting Language,' this dynamic scripting language was developed by Larry Wall in 1987 and borrows features from C, AWK, and sed — which language?
Perl is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language.
Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and often spread by flea bites, this disease comes in pneumonic, bubonic, and septicemic forms — what is it?
Plague (disease) is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. There are three forms of plague, each affecting a different part of the body and causing associated symptoms.
Including raccoons, coatis, kinkajous, and ringtails, this New World mammal family within the order Carnivora is made up mostly of omnivores — what family is it?
Procyonidae is a New World family of the order Carnivora. Procyonidae ( PROH-see-ON-i-dee) is a New World family of the order Carnivora.

This genus of roughly 1,750 flowering plant species, found worldwide mostly in temperate and mountainous regions, includes a tenacious creeping species common in European gardens as well as bulbous and meadow-dwelling relatives. What are these plants commonly called?
Ranunculus is a large genus of about 1750 species of flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae.
Native to West Africa and later naturalized across Asia and the West Indies, this plant's stems yield fibre while its calyces are steeped for a popular infusion — what is it?
Roselle (plant) (Sabdariffa gossypiifolia) is a species of flowering plant in the genus Sabdariffa that is native to Africa, most likely West Africa.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Pythons and boas of this limbless reptile group still carry a tiny pelvic girdle and vestigial leg-stubs near the cloaca, hinting at long-lost legs. What animal is this?
Snake are elongated legless reptiles of the suborder Serpentes.
This group of cartilaginous fish spans eleven families and roughly 220 species, from tiny river-dwellers to giant manta and devil rays — what group of fish is it?
Stingray are a group of rays, a type of cartilaginous fish.
Born in 1946, this American serial killer often posed as an authority figure or feigned injury to lure young women to his car before assaulting and murdering them — who was he?
Ted Bundy (n Cowell; November 24, 1946 - January 24, 1989) was an American serial killer who kidnapped, raped and murdered dozens of young women and girls throughout 1974, 1975, and 1978.
This muscular organ in the mouth manipulates food for chewing and swallowing, serves as the body's primary organ of taste, and also enables human speech — what organ is it?
Tongue is a muscular organ in the mouth of a typical tetrapod.
At just 26, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth 48 times solo aboard Vostok 6 in 1963. Who is she?
Valentina Tereshkova (born 6 March 1937) is a Russian engineer, politician, and former Soviet cosmonaut.

Dubbed the "father of English geology," this man created the first detailed geological map of an entire country — yet his humble background got him snubbed by scientists and even landed him in debtors' prison. Who was he?
William Smith (geologist) (23 March 1769 - 28 August 1839) was an English geologist, credited with creating the first detailed, nationwide geological map of any country.
A legendary Heian-era court diviner and astrologer, this figure lived 84 years free of illness, fueling belief in mystical powers — a Kyoto shrine bears his name today. Who is he?
A shortened-fuselage version of a popular narrow-body jetliner family, this aircraft entered service with Swissair in April 1996 and carries up to 156 passengers — which model?
Airbus A319: Airliner, shortened variant of the A320 family.
Sold under the brand name Xanax, this fast-acting benzodiazepine is most often prescribed for panic disorder and generalized anxiety — what drug is it?
Alprazolam: Benzodiazepine medication. Alprazolam is most commonly prescribed in the management of anxiety disorders, especially panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
Likened to a bubble or balloon, this outward bulge forms at a weak spot in a blood-vessel wall and grows ever more dangerous as it risks rupture — what is it?
Aneurysm: Bulge in the wall of a blood vessel. An aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.
This genus of orb-weaving spiders, encompassing the European garden spider and the barn spider among its 500-plus species, was named by an 18th-century Swedish naturalist in 1757 — which genus?
Araneus: Genus of spiders. The genus was erected by Carl Alexander Clerck in 1757.
Found from the Labrador Sea to the Barents Sea and able to live up to 25 years, this widely eaten fish can occasionally top 180 centimeters and 50 kilograms — what species is it?
Atlantic cod: Species of fish. The Atlantic cod (pl.: cod; Gadus morhua) is a fish of the family Gadidae, widely consumed by humans.
Bred in Britain to hunt rabbits and hares, this scent hound's keen nose also makes it a popular detection dog for smuggled food at airports — which breed?
Beagle: Breed of small scent hound. The Beagle is a British breed of scent hound, similar in appearance to the much larger foxhound.
Colloquially called a buffalo in the US and Canada, this large bovine is actually more closely related to yaks and cattle than to true buffalo — which animal?
This white crystalline sodium borate dissolves in water to form a basic solution and finds uses as a pesticide, a soldering flux, and an ingredient in glass and pottery glazes — what mineral is it?
Borax: Boron compound, a salt of boric acid.
Caused by heat, electricity, chemicals, friction, or radiation — and most often the result of scalding at home — what type of skin injury is classified from first- to higher-degree severity?
Burn: Injury to flesh or skin, often caused by excessive heat.
Nicknamed for its heart-shaped seed pods, this mustard-family weed is considered protocarnivorous because its seeds ooze a mucilage that traps nematodes — which species?
Capsella bursa-pastoris: Species of flowering plant in the mustard family.
Which biological process oxidizes nutrients using an electron acceptor such as oxygen to generate ATP, the universal energy currency of life?
Cellular respiration: Process of releasing energy from nutrients using inorganic electron acceptors.

The second-lightest halogen, this yellow-green gas is so reactive it has the highest electron affinity of any element and once fascinated medieval alchemists heating chloride salts — which element is it?
Chlorine: Chemical element with atomic number 17 (Cl)
Striking at the same hour every day for weeks at a time, usually around one eye, this excruciating neurological condition is considered one of the most painful known to medicine — what is it?
Cluster headache: Neurological disorder. The disease is considered among the most painful conditions known to medical science.

Native to Europe and North Africa, this member of the carrot family can grow to 8 feet tall, with hollow stems blotched dark maroon and a distinctly foul smell carried on the wind — which highly poisonous plant is this?
Conium maculatum: Poisonous plant. The plant is herbaceous, with no woody parts, and has a biennial lifecycle.
This practice of secure communication sits at the intersection of math, computer science, and electrical engineering, and underpins e-commerce and chip-based payment cards — what is it called?
Cryptography: Practice and study of secure communication techniques.

Also nicknamed 'the bends,' this diving-related condition happens when dissolved gases form bubbles in body tissue during a too-rapid ascent, often settling painfully in the knees and elbows — what is it called?
Decompression sickness: Disorder caused by dissolved gases forming bubbles in tissues.

He didn't just arrange the known elements — he left gaps and boldly predicted the properties of three undiscovered ones, later vindicated by germanium, gallium, and scandium. Which Russian chemist was he?
Born in 1869 into an old Anglo-Irish scientific family in Dublin, she is considered the world's first woman medical physicist — who was she?
Edith Anne Stoney: Anglo-Irish medical physicist. Edith Anne Stoney (6 January 1869 – 25 June 1938) was an Irish physicist.
Caused by mutations in any of sixteen genes that weaken the skin's structural attachment layers, this rare inherited condition causes painful blistering from the slightest friction — which disease?
Epidermolysis bullosa: Rare medical conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.
This small woodland bird has blue-gray upperparts, a black eye-stripe, and famously plasters the entrance to its tree-hole nest with mud if it's too large — what is it?
Eurasian nuthatch: Small passerine bird species.
Discovered in the fallout debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952 and named for a pioneer of nuclear physics, this element 100 is the heaviest you can make by neutron bombardment. What is it?
Fermium: Chemical element with atomic number 100 (Fm)
This American physician-scientist led the Human Genome Project before directing the NIH for over a decade under three presidents — who guided the mapping of our DNA?

Named after a long-nosed, insect-eating African animal, this 1960s supersonic fighter-bomber pioneered variable-sweep wings and automated terrain-following radar under Robert McNamara's TFX program. What aircraft is it?
General Dynamics F-111 Aardvark: Family of strike aircraft developed in 1960s.
With the symbol Au and atomic number 79, this soft, dense element is so unreactive that only platinum sits below it — and it often turns up as native nuggets in riverbeds. What is it?
Gold: Chemical element with atomic number 79 (Au). Chemically, gold is a transition metal, a group 11 element, and one of the noble metals.
Combined with obstetrics as a joint medical specialty and touching on everything from family planning to pelvic reconstructive surgery, which field focuses on the female reproductive system?
Gynaecology: Medical area for women's reproductive health.

Often triggered by a preceding throat infection, this childhood autoimmune disease causes raised skin bruising, joint pain, and sometimes kidney trouble from IgA immune-complex deposits — what is it called?
Henoch–Schönlein purpura: Autoimmune vascular inflammatory disease.
Defined today as exactly 3,600 seconds, this unit of time was originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East — which unit?
Hour: Unit of time equal to 60 minutes.
Native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the Caspian region, this mint-family shrub has long been used in traditional herbal medicine as an antiseptic and cough reliever — which plant?

Hyssopus officinalis: Species of plant. Hyssopus officinalis or hyssop is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
An English polymath who was also an alchemist and theologian, he shares credit with Leibniz for inventing calculus and wrote the Principia — who is he?
Part of a four-person extremist cell known for English accents, this Kuwaiti-born militant appeared in Islamic State videos before being killed in a 2015 drone strike near Raqqa — who is he?
Jihadi John: Kuwaiti-British terrorist and ISIS executioner (1988–2015)
Named for a district in Turkey's Sivas Province, which large livestock guardian breed has been exported to Africa to protect flocks from cheetahs?
Kangal Shepherd Dog: Turkish breed of dog. The Kangal Shepherd Dog or Turkish Kangal (Turkish: Kangal Çoban Köpeği) is a traditional Turkish breed of large livestock guardian dog.

Native to the tropical Americas, this flowering shrub was carried to Europe by Dutch explorers and later brought to Goa by the Portuguese, becoming a notorious invasive weed across some 50 countries — which plant?
Lantana camara: Species of plant. Lantana camara (common lantana) is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family (Verbenaceae), native to the tropics of the Americas.
Also called May bells or Our Lady's tears, this woodland plant's sweetly scented white bell-flowers hide a dangerously poisonous secret — which flower?
Lily of the valley: Species of flowering plant in the asparagus family.
This best-known stag beetle species in Western Europe lends its genus its very name, and is currently listed as Near Threatened — what is it?
Lucanus cervus: Species of beetle. L. cervus is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

One of the most colorful mammals alive, this West African monkey sports vivid red-and-blue facial skin and lives in huge groups called 'hordes' — though long mistaken for a baboon, it's actually closer kin to mangabeys. What is it?
Mandrill: Species of Old World monkey from Africa.

This elephant-sized extinct genus of South American ground sloths, whose type species weighed up to four tonnes, was first identified from a fossil found on an Argentine riverbank in 1787 — which genus?
Megatherium: Genus of extinct ground sloth. The first (holotype) specimen of Megatherium americanum was discovered in 1787 on the bank of the Luján River in what is now northern Argentina.
Sold as Versed, this benzodiazepine sedates rather than knocks you out, can be sprayed up the nose or squirted in the cheek, and famously causes anterograde amnesia — which drug?
Midazolam: Benzodiazepine used for anesthesia and procedural sedation.
The platypus and the four species of echidna are the only living mammals in this order that lay eggs rather than bear live young — what is it called?

Dropped from a B-52 and boosted by a modified Pegasus rocket stage before its own scramjet took over, this experimental hypersonic craft still holds the record for fastest jet-powered flight at about Mach 9.6 — what is it?
NASA X-43: Unmanned US experimental hypersonic aircraft, 1991-2000.

Named for a mythological daughter of Tantalus, this silvery transition metal with atomic number 41 was once called columbium and is now prized as a nickel-free option in hypoallergenic jewelry — which element?
Niobium: Chemical element with atomic number 41 (Nb)
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz and built an early radio receiver he named the "coherer" — who was he?
Oliver Lodge: English physicist and electrical engineer (1851–1940)
Discovered in 1802 and named after a newly found asteroid, this silvery-white platinum-group metal is prized for cleaning up automobile exhaust in catalytic converters — which element?
Palladium: Chemical element with atomic number 46 (Pd)
This psychiatric paraphilia involves a primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children, with diagnostic criteria extending the cutoff age to thirteen — which disorder?
Pedophilia: Sexual attraction to prepubescent children. The DSM requires the arousal pattern must be present for 6 months or longer, while the ICD lacks this requirement.
This branch of linguistics studies how spoken languages organize meaningful sound units — the kind of contrast that separates 'bat' from 'gnat' — what field is it?
Phonology: Study of sound organization in languages.

Proposed in 1904 and finally proven a century later using Richard Hamilton's Ricci flow techniques, this problem asks whether any loop-shrinkable finite 3D space must be a hypersphere — which famous problem?
Poincaré conjecture: Theorem in geometric topology.
Nearly odorless with a faintly sweet taste, this diol is approved as a food additive under E-number E1520 and serves as a solvent vehicle in many medications — which compound?
Propylene glycol: Chemical compound. Propylene glycol (IUPAC name: propane-1,2-diol) is a viscous, colorless liquid.
Also known as the holly oak, this large evergreen tree native to the Mediterranean produces acorns that mature within a single summer — which species is it?
Quercus ilex: Oak tree species native to the Mediterranean.

Almost exclusively affecting girls and emerging by 18 months of age, this genetic disorder — usually caused by a mutation in the MECP2 gene — brings language and coordination loss along with repetitive hand movements. What is it?
Rett syndrome: Genetic brain disorder. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a genetic disorder that typically becomes apparent after 6–18 months of age and almost exclusively in girls.

Also called 'German measles,' this vaccine-preventable viral infection is usually mild but can cause severe birth defects — including cataracts and deafness — if a mother catches it early in pregnancy. What disease is it?
Rubella: Human viral disease. Rubella, also known as German measles or three-day measles, is a vaccine-preventable infection caused by the rubella virus.
Named after the Latin word for a small shovel, this flat triangular bone connects the upper arm bone to the collarbone and forms the back of the shoulder girdle — what is it?
Scapula: Bone that connects the humerus and clavicle.
Built with a ribless cartilage skeleton, skin-covering dermal denticles and five to seven gill slits per side, these fish first appeared back in the Devonian — what are they?
A hygroscopic crystalline powder (formula NaNO2) and the most industrially important salt of its kind, this compound is most familiar to us cured into processed meats. What is it?
